newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO says gaps wide in tense Hebron talks.
newsitem.headline: PLO says gaps wide in tense Hebron talks.

text.p: The United States struggled on Wednesday to salvage an Israel-PLO deal for the West Bank town of Hebron after Palestinians called talks "extremely tense" with "very wide" gaps.
U.S. Middle East mediator Dennis Ross continued his efforts to nail down a long-elusive accord on an Israeli handover of 80 percent of the volatile town to Palestinian self-rule.
But both sides said on Wednesday the sticking point had less to do with Hebron than with three further transfers of West Bank areas to Palestinian control.
The Arab world views a Hebron deal as a test of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's commitment to the peace deals he inherited from the government ousted last May.

"The gaps are still very wide," Nabil Abu Rdainah, an aide to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, told Reuters. Arafat's spokesman described five hours of late night talks between Arafat and Ross on Tuesday as "extremely tense."
Ross held another round of talks with Netanyahu in Jerusalem on Wednesday and was due to shuttle to Gaza in the evening to meet Arafat.
The handover of the town, where 400 Jewish settlers live or study among more than 100,000 Palestinians, has been put off for 10 months largely because of Israeli security concerns.

A 1995 interim peace deal binds Israel to complete the final handover of mostly rural areas by September of this year. Netanyahu wants to link it to talks due to be completed by May 1999 on a final Israeli-Palestinian peace arrangement.

Netanyahu's adviser David Bar-Illan said the Hebron talks would pale in comparison to negotiations on thornier issues, including the fate of the 130,000 Jews who live in settlements scattered among the two million Arabs in the West Bank and Gaza.
"How do we secure their safety if we are not to keep areas around them or areas leading to them?" Bar-Illan said.
Netanyahu complained again on Tuesday that he had inherited a "bad" and "porous" agreement that fell short of providing security, drawing fire on Wednesday from PLO negotiators.
"How could a man who carries all this vendetta and hatred against the agreement implement it in a positive way?" Hassan Asfour asked on Israel Radio's Arabic service.
Chief PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat insisted a deal could be sealed only when Netanyahu committed himself to the 1995 accord.

"All efforts are being exerted to close the agreement... once the Israeli government will reaffirm its commitment to the agreement signed in September 1995, I think we will not have any obstacles," Erekat told reporters in Jerusalem.
Erekat and Israeli Foreign Ministry Director Eytan Bentsur on Wednesday invited six countries to take part in an international observer force slated to arrive in Hebron after the redeployment.
Norway, Italy, Denmark, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey are to provide personnel for the 180 member force.
